title: Heart & feeling
subtitle: Feeling and thought share a word.
note: Heart and mind overlap in these dictionary senses. This does not mean the words have identical uses or that their speakers share one theory of emotion.

title: Thought
subtitle: Thinking, a thought, the thinking mind.
note: These entries connect mental life with thinking or a thought. Grammar and context determine whether an English translation needs a faculty, an activity or its content.

title: Reason & understanding
subtitle: Judgment, intellect and comprehension.
note: English “mind” can translate terms whose listed senses emphasize reasoning or understanding. The words are alternatives to compare in context, not a scale of intelligence.

title: Spirit & psyche
subtitle: Mental life and spirit overlap.
note: These entries extend beyond an exclusively cognitive gloss. “Spirit,” “psyche” and “soul” themselves need interpretation; their presence in a dictionary does not establish a shared religious doctrine.

title: Brain
subtitle: An organ and mental life share a name.
note: These words have both brain and mind senses. The lexical overlap is evidence about usage; it does not settle the philosophical relation between brain and mind.

title: Attention & care
subtitle: Attending, noticing and taking care.
note: Hausa hankali includes attention and focus. English uses the verb “mind” for attending or taking care. This compares a noun’s senses with a verb’s uses, not identical grammatical categories.

title: Intention & will
subtitle: What someone means or wants to do.
note: Korean 마음 also has intention and will senses. English “mind” can name an intention or inclination. The same Korean word therefore appears here and in Heart & feeling.

title: Memory
subtitle: Remembering is part of mind’s word history.
note: English mind descends through Old English gemynd, associated with memory. “Keep in mind” preserves a remembering use today. This historical example is distinct from the modern-language comparisons elsewhere in the map.
